chunks: He (peace be upon him) said: Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, is not a tyrant to His servants, nor distant from them, nor heedless of them, nor cutting off His mercy from them, nor misguiding His servants, nor arrogant towards them, nor elevated above them. Rather, He is more merciful to them than a parent to their child, more affectionate to them than a mother to her child, closer to them than the vein of the neck, more capable over them than their own self, more knowing of them than they are of themselves, and more loving to them than they are to themselves.

key_terms.حَبْلِ الْوَرِيدِ: The vein of the neck (symbolizing extreme closeness)
key_terms.ظَلَّامٍ: Tyrant or one who does injustice

ai.seo_question: How does Shia theology describe Allah's relationship with His servants in terms of mercy and closeness?
ai.summary: In *Kamal al-Din*, Shaykh al-Saduq utilizes this hadith to reinforce the Shia doctrine of divine justice (*Adl*), countering the Mu'tazila and Khawarij accusations of *Jabr* (compulsion) or *Tafwid* (delegation) by highlighting Allah's active, intimate care. The vivid comparisons serve to ground theological concepts in relatable human experience, affirming that God's mercy is not abstract but personally accessible to every servant.
